quotes.verbatim_quote: The song has an AABA form, meaning the first theme (or section) is repeated, followed by the second theme, and ending on the original theme.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Defines the AABA form that governs how the student must navigate the chord changes and improvisation across the full song.

quotes.verbatim_quote: NOTE: Whenever | talk about "common keys" throughout this book, | am referring to the concert keys that jazz musicians most commonly play these jazz standards in. These are not necessarily the original keys, but the keys you will need to know these songs in if you want to play them with other musicians
quotes.why_load_bearing: Establishes the book's recurring convention for key references, which affects how every subsequent standard must be read and transposed by non-C instruments.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
This chart is called the Major Diatonic Series of 7* Chords. Essentially, it shows you how chords can be assigned to the different scale degrees of a Major scale.

¥ The top line shows the note names spelling out a C major scale.

Vv The second line shows the quality of chord created when a 7*
chord is harmonized with each scale tone.

VY The third line shows the entire 7** chord name.

¥ The fourth line shows the roman numerals for each scale degree.
The upper case means major or dominant, and lower case means
minor. Ultimately you just need to memorize the quality of chord
for each scale tone.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Defines the foundational reference chart used throughout the book to derive and analyze all chord progressions in major keys.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
This is the Minor Diatonic Series of 7% Chords. It shows you how 7*
chords can be assigned to the different scale degrees of a minor scale.
In this particular case, the natural minor scale is being harmonized, al-
though the 5' degree borrows a note from the harmonic and melodic
minor scales. This is because the V chord is always dominant.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Defines the minor-key counterpart chart and introduces the crucial rule that the V chord is always dominant, regardless of the minor scale used.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
IMPORTANT NOTE: [he Minor Diatonic Series of 7th Chords
is different from the Major Diatonic Series in that it more so rep-
resents common chord choices in the minor tonality than an actual
harmonized scale. It is much more complicated to come up with
a true scale to harmonize because there are the three different
minor scales to consider.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Issues an explicit rule distinguishing the minor chart's use as a practical reference rather than a rigorous harmonization, preventing a common theoretical misapplication.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
Major and minor keys that share the same key signature are called rel-
ative keys. Essentially, they share the exact same notes as each other.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Defines the term 'relative keys,' which is the central harmonic concept organizing the entire analysis of Autumn Leaves.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
From the minor key you can either memorize its relative key or use this
trick: think a major key a minor 3% up from the minor key (or vise-versa).
quotes.why_load_bearing: Gives a practical rule of thumb for identifying relative keys that students can apply across all 12 keys when analyzing or transposing jazz standards.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
When it comes to jazz, there is no more important chord progression
to know than the ii-V-l. You will see it come up time and time again,
and so you need to be able to recognize it right away, and of course,
quotes.why_load_bearing: Establishes the ii-V-I as the highest-priority harmonic pattern for the student to internalize, framing every subsequent standard analysis in the book.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
The IV chord in a minor key is usually minor, but jazz musicians are constantly turning minor chords into dominant 7
chords. You'll see that happen a lot more throughout our studies!
quotes.why_load_bearing: States an idiomatic jazz harmonic rule -- the conversion of diatonic minor chords to dominant 7ths -- that recurs throughout the repertoire covered in the book.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
Guide tones are notes within a chord structure that both help define a
chord, and can be used to transition to another chord melodically.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Defines the guide-tone concept that anchors the book's first and recurring improvisational technique.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
In jazz, the guide tones are almost always the 3rds and 7ths of each
chord.
quotes.why_load_bearing: States the specific rule identifying which chord tones function as guide tones, giving the student a concrete and universally applicable selection criterion.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
The 3rds and 7ths define the chords in this progression. 7" chords are
built: Root-3'9-5%-7". The root is never altered, and the 5" is never al-
tered unless it is a half-diminished or fully diminished 7% chord. Even
still, the 5% is not a strong note in the chord. But the 3% and 7* are
pivotal in defining whether a chord is major, minor, dominant, half-di-
minished, or fully diminished.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Explains the theoretical reason the 3rd and 7th are chosen as guide tones, teaching students why these specific intervals carry the most harmonic information.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
Voice leading is the smooth melodic movement of notes (or voices)
from one chord to the next.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Defines voice leading as a concept, setting up the practical demonstration of how guide tones resolve stepwise through the ii-V-I.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
Notice how the 7* of each chord resolves to the 3 of the next chord.
It happens to work perfectly this way because the chords are cycling
in 4ths. But the basic concept is the closest step-wise motion you can
make from the 7' of a chord in this ii-V-l, is the 3 of the next. That's
voice leading.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Articulates the specific voice-leading rule -- 7th resolves to the 3rd of the next chord -- that is the mechanical core of the guide-tone technique taught here.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
It's a great practice to play them isolated with either half notes or
quarter notes through the entire form of a song, and so that is precise-
ly what we are going to do.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Prescribes the specific drill format -- isolated half or quarter notes through the full form -- for internalizing guide tones on any jazz standard.
